name: Khwarshi
confidence_why: Khalilova 2009 describes weight-sensitive stress for the Kwantlada variety (final syllable when closed, otherwise penult), but Kibrik and Kodzasov 1990 state that Inkhokwari has no word stress and a system of syllable tones, Lomtadze 1998 (as reported by Borise 2021) gives initial or final stress with syllable weight irrelevant, and Borise 2021 concludes there is no consensus on Khwarshi stress.

catalog_quote: 2.5. Word stress. Word stress can be based on the syllabic structure of words and on the morphological principle. 2.5.1. Syllabic structure. The stress is penultimate in the disyllabic and polysyllabic words of CV/VCV structure, i.e. the stress is pretonic. ... The stress is on the final syllable of CVC structure in disyllabic or polysyllabic words: ... So the basic pattern for word stress is that stress falls on the pre-final syllable when the final syllable is open and on the final syllable when it is closed, i.e. heavy syllables attract the stress. (pp. 34-35) ... The stress is phonemic, i.e. it distinguishes words: ... Note that the stress in the imperative forms is always on the first syllable no matter what the syllabic structure of the verb is (p. 37). [Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 328, village Inkhokwari, 'Слог и просодия'] 3. Система слоговых тонов стандартна: H, L, F, R. ... В двусложных словах преобладает схема HL, однако имеются и другие схемы ... 4. Словесное ударение отсутствует, фразовый акцент тяготеет к началу слова.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable when it is closed (CVC), otherwise on the penultimate syllable; heavy (closed) final syllables attract stress. Overlaid on this is a morphological principle: some open-syllable suffixes attract stress (ERG -i, INF -a, PST.W -i, NEG -bi, GEN of pronouns), others never do (PRS -še, PL -bo/-ba, IMP -o/-a/-e, adjectivisers -xu/-tu, NMLZ -ɬi, PL.ADJ -t'a, PST.PTCP -u/-gu); imperatives are always initial-stressed; oblique stems are often derived by shifting stress from penult to ultima (sec. 3.1.3.2.1.1, p. 55). Stress is phonemic (ís-o 'say-IMP' vs isó 'that.GEN1').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Footnote 13, p. 36: in polysyllabic comparative-case forms like himón-ƛ'ozí 'primary stress is on the second syllable, and the secondary stress is on the final syllable'; otherwise 'polysyllabic words which can distinguish a primary and secondary stress pattern need further investigation' (p. 35).
new_statements.exceptions: Genitive 2 of nouns (final open syllable) can also carry ultimate stress; stress-attracting vs non-attracting open-syllable suffixes listed p. 36; pronominal genitives stressed on final open syllable (diyó, isu-ló); imperatives fixed initial regardless of syllable structure (p. 37); Imnaishvili 1963: 22 on stress-triggered reduction 'not fully studied'. Conflicting accounts exist: Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 328 (Inkhokwari village) state there is no word stress and describe syllable tones; Testelets 1999: 341 lists only pharyngealization and tone as prosodic features; Lomtadze 1998: 72 (per Borise 2018) says initial or final, weight irrelevant; Borise 2018: 19 concludes 'no consensus'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; citation (Absolutive) forms of nouns follow the syllabic rule, inflected forms follow the syllabic rule plus the morphological principle; long vowels are always in stressed position (p. 23-24). Grammar is based on the Kwantlada dialect (pp. 4, 12), which Khalilova groups with Inkhokwari.
new_statements.identity_note: Khalilova 2009 describes the Kwantlada dialect (no separate glottocode; she groups it with Inkhokwari, Glottolog dialect inxo1238) and uses 'Khwarshi' as a cover term; Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 (pp. 327-328) and Testelets 1999 (pp. 339-346) describe the Inkhokwari-village variety (inxo1238) and report tone with no word stress. No opened source describes stress in Khwarshi Proper (Glottolog dialect xvar1237), which Khalilova (p. 4) and Testelets (p. 340) call the most divergent dialect. Sources disagree (Borise 2018: 19: 'no consensus'): Khalilova = weight-sensitive stress; K&K 1990 = no word stress, syllable tones; Lomtadze 1998 = initial or final, weight irrelevant.

tone_statements.quote: Nikolaev (2000: 154) reports on collective fieldwork carried out in 1974 with S. A. Starostin, A. E. Kibrik, and S.V. Kodzasov, during which Inkhokwari was described as having phonemic tone. ... According to Nikolaev (2000), monosyllabic nominals have a three-way tonal distinction, with ‘rising’, ‘falling’ and ‘rising-falling’ tones; ... Disyllabic words are described as making a distinction between ‘rising-falling’ and ‘falling-rising’ tonal contours. At the same time, Starostin (1978: 88) Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 328) describe Inkhokwari as possessing four tones and no word stress.
